detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators whose public interconnection queues are captured here — MISO, ERCOT, NYISO, SPP, and CAISO — together show 8,381 project requests totaling roughly 1.72 million MW of planned generation and storage waiting to connect to the grid. Because these queues draw from different regions, use different eligibility rules, and count withdrawn or completed projects differently, the figures are not directly addable into a single national picture; each operator's scope note makes clear what is and is not included. What the queues do reveal, taken individually, is the scale of investment pressure accumulating on the grid: MISO alone carries 693,295 MW across 3,827 requests, ERCOT shows 440,018 MW across 1,797 requests, and even the comparatively smaller CAISO queue holds 71,682 MW across 265 active requests.

For readers tracking AI data center infrastructure, the fuel-type breakdowns inside those queues are the most relevant signal. Storage and gas — the two resource types most directly tied to always-on, dispatchable load — are growing visibly in the regions where data center construction is heaviest. ERCOT's queue contains 160,906 MW of storage and 76,751 MW of gas, the largest gas figure of any operator in this snapshot. CAISO's queue is dominated by storage at 46,944 MW. SPP shows 53,412 MW of storage and 47,392 MW of gas. These are not data center demand figures; they are generation and storage projects that developers are betting will be needed, and the concentration of storage and gas in Texas and the broader south-central and western grids tracks where data center campuses are expanding.

The commercial electricity sales data reported to EIA for June 2026 — covering Arizona, California, Georgia, Illinois, Ohio, Oregon, Texas, and Virginia — shows Texas leading at 15,754 thousand MWh and Virginia at 7,771 thousand MWh in commercial-class sales, with California at 10,025 thousand MWh; because data centers are billed overwhelmingly in the commercial class, these figures serve as a rough proxy for load concentration but are not a direct measurement of data center consumption alone. Average commercial prices ranged from $8.66 per MWh in Texas to $27.33 per MWh in California across those states in that period. Watch whether ERCOT's storage queue share continues to outpace its solar additions in coming monthly reports, as a sustained shift toward dispatchable storage over intermittent generation would be a clearer indicator that grid planners are building specifically for firm, around-the-clock load rather than for general renewable policy targets.
